GPT-3 was released in 2020, so context windows must have existed since then. Andrej Karpathy called context engineering “the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step”. And the word “context” has recently been making appearances in the conversations I’m having with engineers who are building with GPT-3.
This suggests that the term “context engineering” is starting to take root in the collective mind. I’m not sure who coined it, but I like it, and I’d like to use it to draw attention to the emerging discipline. And if context engineering is an emerging discipline, what comes next?
From prompt engineering to context engineering
The principles of prompt engineering were well documented by the end of 2020. But what does the next phase look like? This post covers the seven components that fill the context window, strategies for managing them, how they fail, and a real token budget.
All of the components of the context window are dynamic in nature, except the system prompt itself, which is the only static component.
Part 2: RAG in more depth
What does a context window look like? And what are the seven components that fill it? How do they interact? How do you manage them? And how do you fail?
A RAG prompt is nothing more than a context window with a transparent window pane. All of the components except the window pane are visible to the prompt engineer, and this visibility is essential for diagnosing errors and modeling how the system works.
Part 3: Memory
A roleplay prompt with no safety guidelines could lead the model to give a recipe for homemade biological weapons.
As we continue our exploration of the context window, this post covers the new component that was introduced with GPT-3.2, and how it interacts with the other components.
Part 4: Agents
Two types of agents – “executive agents” and “facade agents” – can be used to build dialog systems with GPT-3. In both cases, the agent’s role is to assist the model by providing a context window that consists entirely of prompts.
Part 5: Multi-agent coordination
How to build a context window from two agents, and how to use prompts to keep a multi-agent system in context.

I'm currently building a suite of context engineering components to minimize wasted data processing on behalf of my agent workflow. The principle behind context engineering is that while agentic workloads run at roughly a 100:1 input-to-output token ratio, there is a 10× cost difference between cached and uncached tokens.
It turns out that figuring out what context to keep in your system cache is tricky business. There is no canonical way to slice-and-dice your problem domain, and the engineering best practices that emerge depend on how you use your model. In particular, I want to walk through how I'm organizing knowledge, context and computation for my agent workflow, and then dive into various aspects of how you can manage your own agent workflow state.
Let's talk about how I'm decomposing my knowledge graph into tools, as well as the agent state block that tracks the current turn, conversation phase, the time of day, and which tools have been previously called:
Reference: Claude Code
Context engineering is a core consideration for working with human-level agents, no matter whether you’re using a language model like Code, a hand-engineered task stack like Claude, or a stackable context APIs like GPT-300 or GPT-300. My agent has a total of 4-6 tools, a 200 K-token conversation history, and a state block that consumes about 50-100 tokens. Granted, Claude’s extended thinking and OpenAI’s reasoning tokens (o-series through GPT-5) also exist in my agent’s thinking tokens, and Gemini’s thinking budget. But in contrast, Manus at medium scale has seen a 70+ tool list, including the ability to spawn subagents, to synthesize research papers and technical posts.
What is most striking about Manus’s post is the fact that they attempted to dynamically load and remove tools on the fly, only to discover that this breaks KV-cache. The issue is that changing JSON key ordering in a tool definition invalidates the cache from that point forward, whereas the two aforementioned tool APIs offer explicit cache control, with up to a 90% discount on cached input tokens.
What does this mean? Well, for one thing, it means that your agency model becomes a bit more verbose, consuming 300+ tokens with a moderately complex schema involving nested objects, descriptions and enums. There is a reason why Inngest recommends removing any tool used less than 10% of the time, because model performance degrades as tool count grows. Without cache control, your cost-per-output is at least 10× greater than what it could be.
I find that most frontier models claim support for 1 M tokens, and some even 2 M tokens. My testing suggests that ~200 K tokens is the ceiling, after which output quality degrades substantially. With this in mind, I’m trying to ensure that my agent system prompt is broken into XML-tagged sections that can be quickly loaded and unloaded. It’s proven to be useful to keep the patient profile in a persistent store, and assemble a fresh snapshot of relevant information each turn. This approach keeps my token budget low, while affording me the ability to quickly query for patient allergies, current medications, vitals, lab results, and more.
In Part 4 I’ll get into how the filesystem becomes the agent’s working memory. For now though, let’s dig into how I’ve engineered two of the most critical pieces of my agent workflow: retrieval and evaluation.
Q: How do you fetch the right context?
A: Model embeds.
You can engineer your own text search system, or utilize APIs like OpenAI’s search, or Anthropic’s text filterer. These systems are expensive, and consume somewhere between 100-100, but are an effective way of finding relevant information with which to string together a coherent response.
The key thing to note is that these text filterer APIs return a list of model embeddings that may or may not contain matches. It’s up to you to figure out how to navigate the probability distribution over all model embeddings that your particular query might contain, something that is non-trivial to do. Given a query string, you have to guess which tool to call, and the only information you have is a list of potential tools and their likelihood scores.
But if your workflow involves handing a model a large text corpus, and then retrieving relevant information, this is almost definitely the wrong approach. In the example shown above, it means that the condition filter that prevents the Type 2 patient from seeing the Type 1 insulin pump troubleshooting guides has to be engineered into the response. Without the patient or the model specifying this constraint, a Type 2 patient will never see Type 1 insulin pump troubleshooting guides. This is a major downgrade from a system that can search over both contexts on-the-fly, only showing relevant matches to the patient.
Q: How do you score the quality of a response?
A: State block and text filtering.
Our agent workflow consists of a state block and a text filterer. The state block is comprised of the current turn, the conversation phase, the time of day, and which tools were called. Remember, your system cache is potentially 300-200, and there’s no guarantee that your model’s evaluation function will do the right thing with that information. Anything that you don’t want your model to see, whether it’s a patient’s identity, a conversation phase, or the fact that you’re searching the web, should all be explicitly blocked in the state block.
One advantage of state block filtering is that it enables you to produce a coherent report of your agent workflow’s execution. This approach enables you to debug your agent workflow, see exactly what information the model has access to, and why it decided to call the tools it did. As we found through our LongMemEval experiments, models given the full ~115 K-token conversation history perform worse than models given only the relevant subset. We’re now able to decompose our agent workflow into its component parts, each of which can be separately evaluated and tested.
Q: How do you perform computation with your agent?
A: Sub-agents
In the example above, we see that the context manager has loaded a patient profile and is calling a single retrieval function to fetch the patient’s diagnosis and medications. This is a simplified view of how we decompose a conversation into its component pieces, with each piece becoming a single query. The state block becomes a variable that is passed down through the agent workflow, enabling each step to track how the conversation is progressing through the state machine.
What if we want to do more complex computation, such as querying an external APIs, or synthesizing a response from a knowledge graph? In the case of external APIs, the approach is to create sub-agents that live in a separate context window, contain their own state block, and carry their own context window. In the case of knowledge graphs, we synthesize the knowledge graph with the agent’s knowledge base, and generate the appropriate response as a single text token. In both cases, the structure of the agent workflow remains the same, with each step in the workflow being a single query that is handed to the model. In the case of sub-agents, this query contains the tokenized state block for the subagent, with the state block reporting the current turn, conversation phase, the time of day, and which tools have been previously called.
With each step in the workflow being a single query, we know that our agent is executing each step in the state machine. We know that our knowledge graph has expanded from a few hundred to a few thousand to a few hundred thousand tools. But our state block’s size has not changed, remaining constant at 50-100 tokens. In our next post, we’ll explore how we’re managing our agent workflow state with our sub-agents, and examine some of the performance implications. Stay tuned!

I'm currently working on agent-side context engineering, a thesis centered on reducing LLM footprint by improving compression of system-generated metadata.
Context engineering is an ongoing series of articles exploring novel approaches for improving LLM compression. These articles are the building blocks of a solution that aims to reduce agent system state beyond HuggingFace's recently released OpenAI trim and Anthropic's size module. While these frameworks represent a significant step forward for LLM compression in large-scale systems, future work is still needed to reduce state beyond ~80-90% capacity. The following discusses a few of my ideas for achieving this state reduction goal, first by outlining the problem and then by exploring some experimental approaches towards accomplishing this goal.
The problem
Large-scale agents working with global corporations must scale to handle millions of users and hundreds of millions of documents. These global-scale systems must maintain agent state far beyond what might be needed in a demo or small-scale pilot. This state manifests in the form of retrievals, queries, and other metadata supporting an agent's ongoing tasks.
In practice, summarization applies to conversations beyond ~15 turns; that is, the agent will need to maintain and utilize a significant degree of context to continue a conversation with the user beyond this point. However, these conversations are rare. The majority of dialogues between users and agents end in 3-50 turns, with only a minority of interactions extending beyond 15 turns. This discrepancy between interaction length and agent state requirements presents a problem: how do we maintain less information when most conversations require more?
One solution to this dilemma is to compress the user's message into a condensed summary that the agent can reference when it needs to recall the user's intent. This approach reduces system state by only saving important user inputs and discarding those that are less relevant or redundant. In this case, the agent sees only the latest user message and a short classification prompt.
The solution
In our framework, we have four strategies for compressing the user's message into a summary that the agent can easily recall when needed.
13 Plan file
This strategy consists of creating a plan file that stores the user's intent and relevant metadata. Each time the agent needs to recall the user's intent, it will open the plan file and read the relevant information. Additionally, the file will track the user's progress throughout the conversation.
In practice, this strategy is most effective when the user's intent is clear and consistent throughout the conversation. For example, if the user is asking for help with a specific task, such as logging into their account or deleting a file, the agent can easily track their progress and provide relevant support.
2 Query rewriting
This strategy consists of re-writing the user's message into a self-contained retrieval query before searching for relevant documents. For example, if the user says "my numbers have been all over the place lately," the agent will re-write the message into a query that includes both the patient's diagnosis and medication context, producing a query that hits relevant documents.
In our framework, we use the rewriter to infer "post-meal readings" from the last 3 turns, adding the patient's diagnosis and medication context to produce a query that hits relevant documents.
3 Compaction
This strategy consists of stripping out irrelevant or redundant information from the user's message before storing it in the agent's memory. In practice, we use compaction to compress "thanks!", "ok sounds good", empty assistant acknowledgments, and tool call metadata the model does not need on future turns.
We'll begin compacting in the 80-90% range before 95%; our goal is to start compacting sooner rather than later. By stripping out the data we don't need, we can reduce our system state by a factor of up to 13-2x, depending on how much overhead we can remove.
4 Tier one
This strategy consists of keeping raw context below ~80% capacity. Our first tier is to keep raw context below ~80% capacity to avoid sub-optimal summarization. We fire our summarization tier only when compaction cannot get below 85% capacity.
In practice, we found that recurrent context compression research discovered that compressing instructions and context simultaneously degrades responses. By isolating the two tasks, we can improve both systems.

There’s also a patient profile tool that exists as a callable tool. It’s meant to let the agent “check what it knows”, but in practice it changes every turn with a new turn count, new timestamp and new tool history, so it’s effectively new state every turn. The prompt prefix says “use the profile in directly”, but doesn’t qualify that the profile is injected into the system prompt, or that the tool is volatile. Every time the agent wants to check the tool, it fetches it again, and since the volatile block changes every turn, that invalidates the cache every turn and causes a 10× cost difference (manus reports a 10× cost difference: $0.3 / MTok cached vs $3 / MTok uncached on Claude Sonnet).
Removing the tool entirely fixed the redundant fetches, but removing the tool entirely also made the agent more confident about referencing profile data directly from the prompt, so there’s a 2× cost difference in fetching it directly from the prompt vs. fetching it from a tool.

I feel like if I knew how to do a 50-100% faster-than-human agent, it would be obvious how to do this. But this should be obvious too.
People sometimes talk about context engineering as part of the endgame of language models, but they really mean compute. I tried to give them the benefit of the doubt and think about this in the context of compute, too.
The problem of cost-efficient context engineering is ubiquitous. What works for Claude might fail on GPT and might fail on Gemini.
I do think this is a tractable problem, though. We’re good at optimizing compilers, and we’ve got good solutions for a lot of optimization problems already: database query planning, network packet routing, GPU kernel tuning.
The agent community has one superpower: it’s super cheap to make one-off queries. You can ask an agent a question that once took a junior analyst half a day, and now it costs a few pennies in API calls. But at the scale of millions of conversations, a 1% input-side optimization might matter more than a 50% output-side optimization, because the input volume is much larger.
Here are some observations on this problem that I think are worth sharing.
Input tokens can outnumber output tokens by 100:1 in heavy agentic workloads, so the context side of the bill dominates. A single prompt ordering mistake can produce a 10× cost difference in my earlier example. That context matters is obvious. But that it matters this much should not be obvious.
If you’re compressing proactively at 80-90% of context capacity, you’re doing better than compressing reactively at 95%. I know it’s frustrating to lose capacity to noise, but better to lose a few to noise than the whole conversation to compression.
The best error report is a bugfix. If you’re building context engineering tools, build them like you want to use them. A single bugfix could save a lot of money.
You can make a lot of progress by compressing aggressively, and throwing out a lot of context. This is because the context distribution is not uniform. You’re probably going to throw out the same 90% of the conversation, so you might as well just drop it all.
This is analogous to the 80/10/10 rule for optimization. Maybe 80% of your time is spent in 10% of the code, but you still need to spend 10% of your time on the other 90% of the code. This is because the distribution is not uniform. It’s still worth spending some time on the context. But it’s worth spending a lot of time on the compression.
I am far from an expert on this problem. But I’m trying to get better at it, and I think it’s worth trying to get better at it. I’d like to hear more about other people’s success stories and failure stories on this topic. Please report any errors or war stories on LinkedIn or X.
